description: Trend passage: same staircase example reworded

pairs.script_span: You spot an uptrend by a run of higher swing highs and higher swing lows, and it stays valid until a swing low breaks. Picture a staircase where every step up is followed by a shorter step back.

passages.text: An uptrend is identified by a sequence of rising swing highs and rising swing lows. The trend is considered intact until a swing low is broken. Traders often illustrate this with a staircase: each step up is followed by a smaller step back.

description: Trend idea with a different example and order

pairs.script_span: Look at the lows first: if every pullback stops above the last one, buyers keep stepping in earlier. Once a pullback undercuts the previous low, that story is over, whatever the highs did.

description: Risk sizing: same three steps reworded

pairs.script_span: First fix how much you can afford to lose on the trade. Then divide it by the gap between your entry and your stop to get the quantity. That way the loss stays the same whatever the share price is.

passages.text: Before entering a trade, decide the amount you are willing to lose. Divide that amount by the distance between entry and stop to obtain the position size. This keeps the loss constant regardless of the instrument's price.

description: Risk sizing with own worked numbers

pairs.script_span: Say a mistake may cost you at most 500 rupees. Your stop is 5 rupees below entry, so 100 shares is the most you can hold. Change the stop distance and the share count changes, not the 500.

description: Volume passage with its fair-crowd simile kept

pairs.script_span: Volume counts the shares that changed hands in a period. When price climbs with volume climbing, it shows participation; when price climbs while volume falls, conviction is weak, like a fair whose crowd is thinning.

passages.text: Volume measures the number of shares traded in a period. Rising price on rising volume is read as participation; rising price on falling volume is read as weak conviction, as with a crowd thinning out at a fair.
